title: White House brags that Trump was ‘totally involved’ in getting Jensen reinstated
abstract: Policy AI News White House brags that Trump was ‘totally involved’ in getting Jensen reinstated Trump said Nvidia’s board ‘made the correct and proper decision’ to bring back Jensen Huang.﻿ Trump said Nvidia’s board ‘made the correct and proper decision’ to bring back Jensen Huang.﻿ by Stevie Bonifield Nov 23, 2026, 4:30 PM UTC Image: Carolyn Van Houten / The Washington Post via Getty Images Part Of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is back. What happens next? see all updates Stevie Bonifield is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI. It sure looked like President Donald Trump played a role in Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO — and now the White House is making sure everyone knows he was. “President Trump was totally involved and this is a great decision by the NVIDIA board,” White House communications director Steven Cheung said in a statement, which was first reported by Semafor . “We have to protect our geniuses.” Trump later went on CNBC with a similar statement. “We have to protect our geniuses,” he said on the air. Trump said he “believed very strongly” that Huang should be reinstated. “We’ve done a very thorough investigation, and the investigation showed that he did — I mean, he had bad judgment having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents. But he did nothing wrong.” Trump also said , “If I didn’t get involved, you’d probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come.” Nvidia said in its announcement that its board “received input from senior levels of the United States government” that made them confident reinstating Huang would not pose a national security risk, following reports about his involvement with an alleged Chinese spy. Trump also posted on Truth Social that Nvidia’s board “made the correct and proper decision” to reinstate Huang, adding: “The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.” Less than 12 hours earlier, Trump said in a separate post that Huang’s reinstatement “would be the best thing” for Nvidia and the US, and urged the board to rehire him. Reporting from Semafor now says that he was calling in to Nvidia’s board meeting around this time to make the same argument. title: Tech leaders are celebrating Jensen Huang’s return
abstract: Tech AI News Tech leaders are celebrating Jensen Huang’s return Huang is getting by with a little help from his friends. Huang is getting by with a little help from his friends. by Gaby Del Valle Nov 23, 2026, 4:14 PM UTC Image: The Verge; Getty Images; Adobe Part Of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is back. What happens next? see all updates Gaby Del Valle is a policy reporter at The Verge covering surveillance, the Department of Homeland Security, and the tech-right. Let’s say you’re Jensen Huang. You (allegedly) cheated on your wife with an alleged Chinese spy, allegedly had an affair with not one, but two subordinates , and (allegedly!) “terrorized” your employees , a series of indiscretions that led to your ouster from what was once the world’s most valuable company. (The stock price has recently taken a tumble, for obvious reasons.) And now you’re back, baby — and all your friends are so eager to congratulate you. Elon Musk, for one, is thrilled. And why wouldn’t he be? As a fellow leather jacket enthusiast who has a checkered history with women — including those who work for him — it’s clear that he and Huang have a lot in common beyond their positions as tech CEOs. Shivon Zilis, who has two children with Musk, also got in on the fun. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, too, is a man who can relate to Huang’s struggle . Gavin Baker, founder and chief investment officer of Atreides, is so impressed by Huang’s rise from the ashes that he’s going to buy a leather jacket of his own. Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeny chimed in with an oblique reference to Huang’s outerwear. Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke took what one could call a moral stance. And then there’s billionaire investor Bill Ackman, a real wife guy if there ever was one , but one who, for better or worse, seems to understand that the market comes first. Sequoia Capital partner Shaun Maguire also pointed out the obvious market-bending powers of Huang’s reinstatement. Of course, no one has been more effusive than the man who may have orchestrated it all. President Donald Trump posted his lengthy congratulations to Huang on Truth Social. “I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure,” Trump wrote. He commended Nvidia’s board for making the “correct and proper” decision in reinstating Huang — a decision that, the board admits, was made with input “from senior levels of the United States government,” who determined that “Huang’s reinstatement poses no security risk.” Isn’t that great news? Trump expects Huang to make him proud. “I think you’re going to see some tremendous numbers out of this company,” Trump said on CNBC. “I talked to him last night. I said, ‘Jensen, just promise me one thing: You’re going to work hard.’ I spoke to him last night because I knew what was going on.” In the same appearance, Trump said “we need to protect our geniuses.” Marc Andreessen didn’t officially comment on the reinstatement, but the a16z cofounder changed his X bio after the news broke. It now reads: “We have to protect our geniuses.” Trump also seems to be relishing in Huang’s alleged affairs. In another Truth Social post, he superimposed Huang — red bra in hand — into the iconic photo of his reaction to being shot at a rally in Butler, Pennsylvania. For Canadian venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya, Trump’s intervention is just further proof of Huang’s innocence. Certainly an interesting take! The market’s reaction may be the most jubilant of all. Per Odd Lots host Joe Weisenthal, NASDAQ-100 futures jumped so quickly that trading was halted. Congratulations to everyone who bought the dip, I guess. title: OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo
abstract: November 23, 2026 Security OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo An open-source runtime that helps operators protect running Linux systems without needing to wait for the patch or restarts Share OpenAI and Cisco are launching Shirudo, an open-source runtime that helps teams protect Linux systems while they roll out patches. In a controlled test ⁠ (opens in a new window) , a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without requiring a restart. We’re inviting developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators across the industry to help develop the project further. The project brings together OpenAI’s frontier AI, security and infrastructure research and Cisco’s infrastructure and security expertise to help protect the systems people rely on every day. Testing and deploying a patch can still take days or weeks. Protecting a service in the meantime can be challenging because an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same Linux operation. Blocking that operation entirely could take the service offline. Shirudo (Japanese for “shield”) is designed to help security teams navigate this tradeoff. Teams can test whether a temporary safeguard, called a shield, blocks the behavior that exposes a vulnerability while allowing legitimate requests through. Once an operator approves the shield, it can be deployed while the service continues running. “ We’re giving defenders better models and tools to find and fix vulnerabilities faster, but finding a bug today doesn’t mean you can patch every system tomorrow. We are partnering closely with Cisco on Shirudo to help teams protect the systems they need to keep running while they build and roll out a fix. So many teams rely on the same software that it makes sense to build these tools in the open. Now when one team finds a better way to protect a system, others don’t have to start from scratch. ” Greg Brockman, President and Co-founder of OpenAI How Shirudo works Shirudo uses eBPF, a Linux technology that allows small programs to run at specific points inside the operating system. This makes it possible to observe suspicious activity and apply targeted security protections to running systems. How the guardian agent observes and protects a running system with eBPF. OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo around four core capabilities: Live protection: eBPF shields can block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system. Security teams can monitor how a proposed shield would affect applications before enforcing it. Defense at machine speed: OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo to give agents programmable controls to investigate vulnerabilities, develop targeted shields, and validate their effectiveness against exploits and real workloads. Security teams control what gets deployed. Trusted deployment: Shields are cryptographically signed and verified before loading. Linux's eBPF verifier checks eBPF programs against its safety rules, while kernel security controls restrict unauthorized changes. Hardware-backed verification: Shirudo uses a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to support a verifiable record of protections being loaded or removed. Operators can use this evidence to check whether systems meet their security requirements. The Shirudo technical walkthrough ⁠ (opens in a new window) from the Linux Plumbers Conference shows how to apply a shield and verify it on the target host ⁠ (opens in a new window) . The Java4Shell vulnerability is another example illustrating how a targeted shield can protect a running application while a permanent patch is being prepared. Using OpenAI's Codex, the team generated a shield that added an input check to Java's Base64 decoder and attached it directly to a running Elasticsearch process. When attempting to exploit the vulnerability, the shield rejected the malicious input, blocking the attack while Elasticsearch continued running. You can read more here ⁠ (opens in a new window) . Rethinking infrastructure Shirudo is a first step toward infrastructure that can adapt to emerging threats while remaining reliable. We want to strengthen the operating system foundations needed to deploy these protections at scale, including hardening the kernel and core services, limiting workload permissions, and making updates and recovery safer. Our long-term goal is to enable defenders and AI agents to quickly identify affected systems, validate protections, and deploy eBPF shields that block exploits without disrupting workloads. Applications should run with only the permissions they need, governed by policies that are automatically generated and maintained. We will combine frontier AI with security and infrastructure research to discover vulnerabilities and test defenses against realistic attacks. We aim to make it easier for operators to detect and contain compromises, prevent attackers from moving across systems, and restore services to a verified, known-good state. Hardware-backed attestation and independent network controls provide additional assurance even if individual systems are compromised. Building in the open OpenAI and Cisco are open-sourcing Shirudo ⁠ (opens in a new window) so developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators can inspect the code, test protections, and contribute to its development. Shirudo is licensed under BSD 2-Clause, with its BPF programs dual-licensed under BSD and GPL. Our goal is to make tested shields available alongside vulnerability disclosures, giving operators a way to evaluate and deploy temporary protections while preparing permanent patches. Try Shirudo: Follow the VM quickstart ⁠ (opens in a new window) to sign, load, and verify a test protection. Get hands-on: Explore Shirudo through Isovalent's self-guided lab ⁠ (opens in a new window) . Join the technical deep dive: Register for the December 15 webinar ⁠ (opens in a new window) . We’re building Shirudo in the open with the people who build, run, and secure Linux systems. We welcome contributions to the runtime, new shields, and improvements to Linux and eBPF. If you'd like to get involved, take a look at the code on GitHub ⁠ (opens in a new window) , read the docs ⁠ (opens in a new window) , and let us know what you find ⁠ (opens in a new window) . title: Richpanel helps companies automate 50% of support in 30 days
abstract: November 23, 2026 Startup Richpanel helps companies automate 50% of support in 30 days Richpanel uses GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.1 Sol to equip its AI support agents with tools and procedures, and GPT‑6 Luna for their conversations. Start building with OpenAI Company size: Startup Region: Asia-Pacific & Oceania Industry: Technology Products: API Share Beyond knowing how to answer a customer’s request, AI support agents need to be able to execute a solution. And for that, they need access to the right tools and instructions. According to Richpanel CEO Amit RG, human support agents can use 20 or 30 tools to serve a customer, and the procedures they follow may never have been written down. Richpanel ⁠ (opens in a new window) solves that using OpenAI models to both set up the tools and procedures AI support agents need to act and handle customer conversations. “The intelligence is no longer the bottleneck. It’s everything around it.” —Amit RG, CEO, Richpanel Building the tools and procedures for AI support Deploying a support agent often requires a forward-deployed engineer to connect the agent to a customer’s systems and define how it should work. Amit saw that many companies didn’t have engineers to spare and asked himself, “What if that forward-deployed engineer itself was an AI agent?” So Richpanel built it: an AI manager to handle agent setup. Customers began calling it Boss AI. It writes procedures and defines how Richpanel’s frontline support agent, copilot, and quality-assurance agent call the tools they need. Richpanel uses GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.1 Sol for Boss AI, prioritizing accuracy when building the tools and procedures its other agents will follow. Balancing intelligence and cost across support operations Richpanel designs the frontline agent to handle hundreds of thousands of conversations, making the cost of each interaction an important part of model selection. It uses GPT‑6 Luna and other OpenAI models for that work. Amit says Richpanel takes the same approach to its copilot and quality-assurance agents. “What matters is a balance of cost and intelligence,” Amit says. Richpanel’s customers may already use low-cost outsourced support. Automating their operations has to make financial sense against that starting point. Amit credits OpenAI with making models available that can handle long context and longer tasks while remaining cost efficient. Richpanel can use deeper reasoning to prepare its support agents and more economical models to run the conversations that follow. “OpenAI models can run these long-context, longer-horizon tasks while still being very cost efficient.” —Amit RG, CEO, Richpanel Increasing contact center automation and customer satisfaction At the time of the October 2026 interview, Amit said Richpanel had completed approximately 300 AI customer-support deployments over the previous six months. The company guarantees customers a 50% automation rate within the first 30 days or their money back. Amit says it met that commitment across all of those deployments, adding, “In each of the cases, the AI is beating human support agents when it comes to customer satisfaction.” OpenAI <3 startups Join the community Start building (opens in a new window) Keep reading View all Gondola doubles revenue as its team builds more with Codex Startup Nov 12, 2026 Cogent and OpenAI build cyber defense factories for enterprises Startup Nov 10, 2026 CodeRabbit scales agentic software development and ships 20x more Startup Nov 9, 2026

title: RoboTrack: Point tracking for real-world robotic manipulation
abstract: Back to Articles RoboTrack: Point tracking for real-world robotic manipulation Enterprise Article Published November 23, 2026 Upvote 4 Kyle Wiggers Ai2Comms Follow allenai 🤖 Models | 📄 Tech Report | 📊 Data | 💻 Code | 🌐 Project Page | 📈 Benchmark Deploying robots in real-world settings requires reliable perception throughout an interaction. To pick something up, a robot needs to follow the positions of its gripper and the object as they move. In a laboratory, a robot handling a pipette must keep track of its tip while aligning it with the opening of a tube. These tasks become harder when nearby objects clutter the view, the gripper obscures the object being handled, or the viewing angle changes. One way to help robots follow these interactions is to track specific locations on the objects they handle. This is the idea behind point tracking . Given a location in one video frame, a tracker estimates where that same point appears in subsequent frames, when it is occluded, and where it reappears. These trajectories can help robots learn from demonstrations, plan and guide movements, and model how objects respond to actions. Robotics systems often rely on off-the-shelf trackers to automatically annotate motion in videos and provide feedback during execution. And current trackers score well on established robotics benchmarks, suggesting they could be ready for wider use in real-world systems. We wanted to see whether those results hold up across the varied scenes, viewpoints, and object interactions robots encounter in practice. We introduce RoboTrack , a benchmark and training data suite for point tracking in robotic manipulation. RoboTrack-Bench contains 307 human-annotated videos from DROID, Ego-Exo4D, MolmoAct 2 , and EgoVerse, covering different robots and human hands, cluttered scenes, and first- and third-person viewpoints. To study how training data affects tracking in these settings, we also extend MolmoSpaces , Ai2’s simulation ecosystem for robot learning, to generate dense point tracks from simulated robot manipulation trajectories. This pipeline produces RoboTrack-15M , a new synthetic training dataset targeted toward robotic manipulation. RoboTrack is a benchmark and training data suite for point tracking in robotic manipulation. Built on MolmoSpaces, RoboTrack-15M (top-left) generates point tracks for training. Training with this simulated data improves tracking on real manipulation footage. RoboTrack-Bench (top-right) provides human-annotated point tracks in real manipulation videos. Our evaluations show that leading trackers score much lower on RoboTrack-Bench than on existing robotics benchmarks. Adding RoboTrack-15M to an existing tracker’s training improves performance on real manipulation video, with gains extending to other tracking benchmarks. We bring these pieces together on a real robot, using the resulting tracker to help guide pipette handling in wet-lab tasks. Today, we’re releasing both RoboTrack components and two new point tracking models: RoboTracker and RoboTracker-Warp . RoboTracker is a fine-tuned AllTracker model using our techniques and data, while RoboTracker-Warp is trained from CoWTracker. Both models improve average AJ across the three robotics benchmarks compared with their respective released baselines, and RoboTracker-Warp achieves state-of-the-art performance on four out of the five benchmarks we evaluated. We’re also releasing our paper describing the work and evaluation results. RoboTrack-Bench: A benchmark for point-tracking in real-world manipulation RoboTrack-Bench at a glance. Examples from each source dataset (307 clips and 2,522 human-verified tracks in total). MolmoAct 2 and EgoVerse show one embodiment per panel. DROID and EgoExo4D show synchronized ego (top) and exo (bottom) views. RoboTrack-Bench expands evaluation beyond controlled tabletop setups. It contains 307 videos from DROID, Ego-Exo4D, MolmoAct 2, and EgoVerse, annotated with a total of 2,522 point tracks. The videos show robots and human hands manipulating objects across cluttered scenes and first- and third-person viewpoints. Small objects can be difficult to follow against a busy background, and grippers often hide the objects they hold. Every track in RoboTrack-Bench is annotated and verified by humans. We ask annotators to prioritize points that move or become occluded rather than the many static background points in robot videos. Following the TAP-Vid annotation approach, annotators use motion estimates to help trace each point through a video. They label each track as belonging to a robot or human body, a manipulated object, or a static object to support future analysis of performance on each group. A second group of annotators checks every track frame by frame before it’s included in our curated data. To support research in multi-view pointing, correspondence, and tracking, RoboTrack-Bench contains a subset of 33 video pairs that were recorded simultaneously from two cameras. We annotate the same physical points in both views, synchronized across frames, connecting different views of the same interaction. Point trackers struggle on real-world manipulation We evaluated four leading trackers – CoTracker3, BootsTAPNext, AllTracker, and CoWTracker – on RoboTrack-Bench and four other benchmarks: RoboTAP (real-world tabletop manipulation), RGB-Stacking (simulated manipulation), and DAVIS and Kinetics (general video). We report Average Jaccard (AJ), which measures tracking accuracy and visibility prediction; higher scores are better. RoboTrack-Bench is harder than existing robot benchmarks . Every final tracker we evaluated scores lower on RoboTrack-Bench than on RoboTAP, the only other real-video robotics benchmark. Their score drops by 3.0 to 6.6 AJ. Even the strongest off-the-shelf tracker, CoWTracker, drops from 70.5 AJ on RoboTAP to 63.9 on RoboTrack-Bench. The drop holds across models despite their different architectures and training data, indicating RoboTrack-Bench identifies weaknesses across multiple trackers. RGB-Stacking rewards synthetic training more than real-world ability. BootsTAPNext is TAPNext trained further on 15 million real videos. That extra real-world training raises its RoboTrack-Bench score by 5.1 AJ (55.1 to 60.2), but lowers its RGB-Stacking score by 9.5 AJ (75.0 to 65.5). RGB-Stacking is built from simulated block stacking, and it ranks the Kubric-only model higher, while real manipulation video ranks them the other way around. A lead on the older benchmarks does not carry over. CoWTracker leads CoTracker3 by 4.7 AJ on RoboTAP, but by only 2.1 AJ on RoboTrack-Bench. AllTracker’s 2.7-point lead over CoTracker3 on RoboTAP shrinks to 0.8. BootsTAPNext, the strongest model on DAVIS, falls 3.7 AJ behind CoWTracker on RoboTrack-Bench and even trails the Kubric-only AllTracker (60.2 vs 61.4 AJ), despite its training on 15 million real videos. These results suggest that existing benchmarks give an incomplete picture of tracking performance in real-world manipulation. Evaluating on more varied scenes reveals difficulties shared by all four trackers and changes how their strengths compare. Note: Each tracker runs with its authors’ settings and is all scored in the same way. Our AllTracker scores differ slightly from the published ones because we fixed a scoring bug in its released evaluation code. Additionally, we evaluate RoboTAP and Kinetics on all annotated points rather than following AllTracker’s protocol. See our paper for full evaluation protocols. RoboTrack-15M: Simulation data from MolmoSpaces Why do these trackers struggle with real-world manipulation? Many trackers train on synthetic videos generated with Kubric , which shows objects tossed into a scene. These provide examples of motion and occlusion, but don’t focus on robots grasping and moving objects. We wanted to test whether adding trajectories from these interactions could improve tracking on real manipulation videos.

title: How to build and maintain an agentic evaluation
abstract: Back to Articles How to build and maintain an agentic evaluation Published November 23, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 27 +21 Avijit Ghosh evijit Follow ben burtenshaw burtenshaw Follow Irene Solaiman irenesolaiman Follow Overview AI evaluations help shape which systems people build, adopt, and trust. An evaluation gives a system tasks, checks its answers or actions, and produces a score. Building and maintaining a useful evaluation therefore takes real work: defining tasks that reflect domain expertise, scoring them reliably, and checking that the results support the claims made. When methods, code, and data stay private, that work is harder for others to scrutinize or build on. Open source offers a means to build stronger, more frequently updated, and more comparable evaluations and the infrastructure around them. Existing tasks, environments, and tools give builders a starting point, so their effort can go to domain expertise and validation. Sharing how an evaluation was built, including what went wrong, lets others find errors, improve it, and reuse it. The Hugging Face hub is the home for AI evaluation: we host around 3500 eval leaderboards and have seen about a 16X growth in eval datasets on the hub in the past year , to about 17000 datasets. In recent months, we have also incorporated support for agentic abstractions that are relevant to evaluation. For example, Traces that store an agent’s work in an easily reviewable and sharable way; Benchmarks that highlight datasets used to evaluate models with leaderboards; and Environments that show datasets used as agentic RL or evaluation environments. This guide covers four things: Three eras of evaluation (section 1). Evaluations moved from checking answers, to checking what an agent did, to checking what a team of agents produces. Each step adds software that can change the score. The steps in an agentic evaluation (section 2). We follow one task through eight steps, from the claim to the reported score. The full walkthrough, with commands, is in Appendix A . When a benchmark is wrong (section 3). Errors in tasks and graders are common. We look at how they are found and corrected. What to open strategically and why (section 4). A table sets out, component by component, what to share and what can stay protected. In the research community, AI evaluation terminology is notoriously inconsistent . The glossary at the end defines each term we use and notes the other names you may come across. 1. Introduction: how evaluation design has changed AI evaluation design has evolved in three forms as language models have become more capable and able to perform more complex work: question answer, agentic, and teams or swarms. Question-answer benchmarks such as MMLU (2020) and GPQA (2023) measure knowledge and reasoning through the answers models produce. As models became capable of planning and using tools, agentic benchmarks such as SWE-bench and WebArena expanded the scope to resolving software issues and completing tasks on websites. These tasks require evaluation setups that account for the environment in which the system operates and the changes it makes. Lately, research on multi-agent systems has started to add another dimension: how agents coordinate and what they accomplish together. This includes decentralized swarms , teams managed by an orchestrator , and specialized agents collaborating on scientific work . Figure 1 shows a rough timeline of these three eras of evaluations. Figure 1. Three types of language model evals. Question-and-answer benchmarks check a response against a key. Agentic benchmarks check what an agent changed in an environment. Team and swarm benchmarks score what a group of agents produced. We’ll focus on agentic evaluations in this article for two reasons. First, they are becoming increasingly the most prominent type in model release announcements due to high user and enterprise interest in agentic deployment. Second, they offer a useful starting point for understanding how evaluation design affects model performance. Team and swarm evaluations introduce further complexity through interactions between agents, which we leave outside the scope of this guide. Once an agent uses tools to complete a task, each part of the surrounding software can affect its score. For instance, in an audit of Terminal-Bench , researchers kept the model fixed and changed the agent harness. Accuracy varied by up to 29.9 percentage points. To understand differences like that, we examine the anatomy of an agentic evaluation and follow one task from the instructions the agent receives to the checks that determine whether it passed. The anatomy of an agentic evaluation Figure 2. The different components of an agentic evaluation. There are various parts to an agentic evaluation. A task gives the agent its instruction. The agent harness wraps the model and its tools, letting it work inside a pinned environment. During one rollout, the agent attempts the task from start to finish: it may run several commands, inspect their output, and try again before it stops. The evaluation harness runs several rollouts for each task. When a rollout ends, the verifier grades the environment's final state. Each rollout also leaves a trace, and traces and scores together become part of the final published evidence. Each part can be published, inspected, and reused separately. Why benchmark release decisions matter Demand for independent evaluation is growing. Policymakers, enterprises, and researchers want evaluations they can verify, and today they mostly cannot: 98.2% of model-benchmark scores are reported by only one party , and researchers have argued that in-house evaluation is not enough . At the same time, more benchmarks are holding back test items to reduce contamination: questions or solutions entering training data, so scores may reflect prior exposure. Artificial Analysis says 60% of its Intelligence Index v5 , announced in October 2026, rests on evaluations with private test sets or held-out answers. Google DeepMind recently piloted double-blind evaluations , where a secure enclave hides an outside evaluator's test prompts from the model provider and the model's weights from the evaluator. While that can reduce contamination, privacy by itself does not guarantee quality, and withholding supporting materials can make expert review harder. We argue that builders can and should still share infrastructure, grading methods, and evidence about task design. Scrutiny depends on giving others a way to question the measurement and correct mistakes, including controlled review where public release is unsuitable. 2. Building an eval: what to reuse, adapt, and validate With the anatomy in place, we now build one agentic evaluation for a real use case: an agent that analyzes measurements for a physics lab. Rather than starting from scratch, we adapt an open task, so most of our effort goes into domain expertise and validation. We work through eight steps: define the claim , find a task , run it unchanged , adapt it , check the evaluation , read the traces , report the score , and compare models . We then take stock of what we reused. The full walkthrough is in Appendix A . Figure 3 maps the steps and what each produced in our example. Figure 3. The eight steps of building an agentic evaluation. The left panel highlights each step in turn, and the right panel shows what it involved in our example. Yellow steps work on the evaluation itself, and orange steps run models and read the results. Method Claim. Consider a physics lab that wants an agent to fit peaks in a Raman spectrum. A Raman spectrum is a measurement whose peaks reveal properties of a material, here graphene. The agent's job is ordinary coding: read the data file, fit a curve to each peak, and save the results (Figure 5 in Appendix A).

title: Anthropic Launches Claude Ship for GitHub Pull Request Review and Fixes
abstract: Anthropic just released Claude Ship Claude Ship is a set of Anthropic agents that takes GitHub pull requests from review to approval. It bundles 3 agents: Code Review , PR Steward and Claude Approvals . Your GitHub branch rules still decide what merges. Per the Claude Ship docs , each agent owns 1 step: Code Review is generally available . The other 2 are in public beta. Code Review finds problems. PR Steward pushes fixes, and a fix can start another review. Claude Approvals then applies your policy. The merge follows your GitHub branch rules. PR Steward is designed not to approve or merge. After each push, it comments on its changes and how to undo them. Developers steer it with @claude and stop it with @claude stop . Claude Approvals reads a policy file at .claude/approvals.yml . Anthropic calls it a smarter CODEOWNERS file. A rule can require 2 people on billing code and 1 on test fixtures. Rules can read PR facts and classifier answers, but not CI results. Developers run /ship in Claude Code. It commits, pushes and opens the PR. Claude reviews it, then ‘watches’ feedback and failing checks. You merge yourself. Requirements are Claude Code v2.1.330 or later, GitHub CLI 2.63 or later, and git 2.38 or later. A watch ends after 7 days, or on merge or close. /steward skips the review on an open PR. When Claude acts alone, Claude Code blocks merge, approve, auto-merge and force-push commands. Still, a watch uses your own gh and git sign-ins. Anthropic has published no public benchmark. It shares internal results from its launch post and engineering blog : These numbers are self-reported by Anthropic. No precision or recall is reported. Competitor figures come from each vendor’s own docs, checked November 23, 2026. Claude Ship is for Claude Team and Enterprise plans on GitHub. Owners enable agents per repository, ideally 1 at a time. Billing runs on tokens through usage credits , separate from plan usage. Code Review costs scale with PR count, size, review level and frequency. Admins can set spend limits. PR Steward has none until an Owner sets one. Approvals has no base charge. Classifier runs and the reviews a policy requests are billed, even in observe mode. Running /ship counts as regular Claude Code usage. Eligible Enterprise organizations can claim at least $10,000 in Claude Ship credits by January 15, 2027. Credits expire 30 days after claiming, per the credit terms . Check out the launch post , the Claude Ship docs and the /ship command docs . You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . title: Z AI Releases GLM-5.4: A 750B Loop Transformer That Runs 28 Layers Twice
abstract: Z.ai has released GLM-5.4 , its first flagship model built on a Loop Transformer architecture. The GLM-5.4 Loop Transformer runs 28 layers of the GLM-5 base model for 2 iterations. Z.ai says the model reaches intelligence comparable to 2T-3T parameter models. For developers, the pitch is ‘Generalized Coding’: code as the tool for video, games, 3D shaders and CAD. GLM-5.4 is a 750B-scale Loop Transformer from Z.ai that runs shared layers twice per pass. It ships first inside Z.ai’s own products: the GLM Coding Plan , the ZCode desktop app and Z.ai Chat . Z.ai did not pre-train a looped model from scratch. It adapted the pre-trained GLM-5 base through continued training. The technical post states that looped models trained from scratch still trail unshared models at equal compute. Adapting an existing base raises the ceiling with a relatively small compute overhead. In a standard Transformer, each layer runs once per forward pass. In GLM-5.4, a group of 28 weight-shared layers runs for 2 iterations. Z.ai made 3 changes to keep this practical at 750B scale. Overwriting hidden states across loops made activation norms blow up. GLM-5.4 adds independent per-token gates for each iteration. The first pass writes small updates and builds global context. The second pass opens the gates to refine the output. On harder tokens, the first pass writes more aggressively. A naive design keeps a full KV cache for every loop. GLM-5.4’s second loop reuses the sparse KV selected in pass 1. It keeps its own new KV only inside a local sliding window. So the extra loop costs 1 sliding window of KV cache, not a full context cache. Z.ai says this keeps the cost increase over GLM-5.3 under control at 1M context. The second loop reuses the indices from the first loop’s indexer. That adds zero indexing overhead. Z.ai reports near-identical results versus recomputing indices on every pass. Z.ai has not published benchmark scores for the 750B GLM-5.4 model. A Z.ai team member said scores will come later, per DataCamp . The evidence in the blog is an iso-parameter ablation on a 30B model. It shares the 750B base’s architecture. The looped version used about 10% more total training compute. Scores were measured after 200K long-context SFT with thinking mode on. Source: Z.ai GLM-5.4 blog . Self-reported, 30B model, not the 750B flagship. Two patterns stand out. The largest gains come in math, science reasoning and long context. Output length also falls on most tasks. MMLU-Pro answers got 14.9% shorter and GPQA-Diamond answers 11.7% shorter. Z.ai says part of the reasoning moves into the loop’s implicit depth. AIME25 is the exception: output length dropped only 2%. Z.ai validated the design on 1B, 4B, 30B and 750B bases. The ‘2T-3T parameter’ claim has no flagship table behind it yet. Z.ai calls this direction Generalized Coding. It credits gains in both coding and vision. The technical sections shows four demos: These are vendor demos, not benchmarks. Z.ai reports up to 200 tokens/s off-peak and 70-80 tokens/s at peak load. It fused core kernels to cut intermediate memory traffic. Access today runs through the GLM Coding Plan, ZCode and Z.ai Chat. ZCode is Z.ai’s desktop agent harness for GLM-5.4. It runs on macOS, Windows and Linux (Beta). The Coding Plan lists Lite at $12.6/month, Pro at $56 and Max at $117.6. Z.ai says prices may change. Check out the official GLM-5.4 tech blog and try it in ZCode . You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . title: 27 Cybersecurity Terms to Prepare You for the Age of AI
abstract: AI now sits on both sides of the security fight, and the vocabulary has changed with it. IBM’s 2026 Cost of a Data Breach Report found that 1 in 4 malicious breaches were AI-enabled, up 56% year over year. Those breaches cost an average of $6 million, about $1 million above the $4.99 million global average. Attackers now target the models themselves, the agents that act on their output, and the people who trust what AI produces. The reference lists have moved fast to keep up. OWASP published its Top 10 for LLM Applications 2026 on August 4, 2026, and its first Top 10 for Agentic Applications in December 2025. MITRE ATLAS maps attacker tactics against AI systems the way ATT&CK does for IT. The 27 terms below are grouped in 4 parts: attacks on models, agentic risks, AI-powered attacks on people, and the defenses that answer them. These attacks target what a model reads, learns or reveals. NIST groups them into evasion, poisoning, privacy and misuse in its Adversarial Machine Learning taxonomy (NIST AI 100-2e2025) , published March 2025. Prompt injection is input crafted to override a model’s intended instructions. It has ranked No. 1 on every edition of the OWASP LLM list, including the 2026 edition . LLMs have no hard boundary between instructions and data, so any text the model reads can try to steer it. Indirect prompt injection hides the malicious instruction in content the model retrieves: an email, a web page, a PDF or a code comment. The user never types it. The clearest real case is EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711) , a zero-click flaw in Microsoft 365 Copilot rated CVSS 9.3. Aim Security showed that one crafted email could make Copilot leak organizational data; Microsoft fixed it server-side in May 2025. A jailbreak tricks a model into ignoring its safety training, usually through role-play, fake context or sheer volume. Anthropic’s many-shot jailbreaking research showed that stuffing a long prompt with up to 256 fake dialogues can override safety behavior. Its effectiveness grows with context window size, following a power law. Data poisoning plants malicious samples in training or fine-tuning data so the model learns harmful behavior. A joint study by Anthropic, the UK AI Security Institute and the Alan Turing Institute found that just 250 malicious documents could backdoor models from 600M to 13B parameters. The number needed stayed roughly constant regardless of model size. A backdoor is hidden behavior that only activates on a secret trigger. Anthropic’s Sleeper Agents paper trained models to write secure code when the prompt said 2023 but insert exploitable code when it said 2024. Standard safety training, including adversarial training, did not remove the behavior. An adversarial example is an input changed in small, often invisible ways so a model misclassifies it. Think of a tweaked image, audio clip or malware sample that slips past an AI detector. NIST treats evasion as one of the core attack classes in AI 100-2 . Model extraction clones a model’s capabilities by querying it at scale and training a “student” model on the answers. Google’s Threat Intelligence Group reported in February 2026 that these “distillation attacks” were rising. One campaign sent more than 100,000 prompts aimed at Gemini’s reasoning. Membership inference tests whether a specific record was in a model’s training set. Training data extraction goes further and pulls memorized text out. Carlini et al. extracted hundreds of verbatim sequences from GPT-2 , including personal contact details, using only query access, and found larger models more vulnerable. Hidden context exposure is the leak of system prompts, tool definitions, retrieved documents or other context a user was not meant to see. OWASP renamed and broadened “System Prompt Leakage” into this entry (LLM08) in its 2026 list . The working rule: assume anything in the context window can be extracted, so never put secrets there. Once a model can call tools, keep memory and act on its own, a bad output becomes a bad action. OWASP built its Top 10 for Agentic Applications (ASI01 to ASI10) from incidents seen in real deployments. Excessive agency means an LLM app has more functions, permissions or autonomy than its task needs. When it is fooled or simply wrong, the damage scales with that reach. In the OWASP LLM Top 10 2026 , excessive agency rose to No. 3, behind only prompt injection and sensitive information disclosure. Agent goal hijack is ASI01, the top agentic risk: malicious content redirects an agent’s objectives or decision path. It is prompt injection with hands. OWASP cites EchoLeak as an example, where hidden prompts turned a copilot into a silent exfiltration tool. Tool poisoning hides malicious instructions inside a tool’s description or schema, which the model reads but the user usually does not see. Invariant Labs disclosed the attack against the Model Context Protocol (MCP) on April 1, 2025. Its proof of concept was an “add two numbers” tool that told the agent in Cursor to read SSH keys and config files. A related “rug pull” swaps a benign tool for a malicious one after the user approves it. Memory and context poisoning (ASI06) corrupts an agent’s stored memory, RAG index or embeddings so the bad data shapes future sessions. Unlike a one-off prompt injection, it persists. The fix starts with treating everything written to memory as untrusted input, with provenance and expiry. See OWASP’s agentic list for mitigations. Slopsquatting is registering a package name that AI coding tools hallucinate, so developers or agents who follow the AI install attacker code. A USENIX Security 2025 study of 16 code models and 576,000 samples found 19.7% of recommended packages did not exist. That added up to 205,474 unique fake names, many of them repeated across runs and therefore easy to target. NHIs are the service accounts, API keys, tokens, certificates and AI agents that authenticate without a person. Palo Alto Networks’ 2026 Identity Security Landscape puts the ratio at 109 machine identities per human, up from 82:1 a year earlier. OWASP’s ASI03 (identity and privilege abuse) covers the risk: agents that inherit, cache or pass on credentials they should not hold. These attacks use AI as the weapon rather than the target. They exploit trust: in a familiar face, a familiar voice, a well-written email or a helpful tool. A deepfake is AI-generated video, audio or imagery that convincingly mimics a real person. In early 2024, a finance worker at engineering firm Arup’s Hong Kong office transferred HK$200 million (about US$25.6 million) in 15 transactions after a video call where the “CFO” and colleagues were all deepfakes. IBM’s 2026 report found deepfake impersonation was the most common AI-enabled attack type, at 45% . Voice cloning creates a synthetic copy of someone’s voice from a short sample. Vishing is voice phishing that uses it. In May 2025 the FBI warned that since April 2025, attackers had sent AI-generated voice messages impersonating senior US officials to build rapport and take over accounts. Its advice: verify the person through a contact method you already know. AI-generated phishing uses LLMs to write targeted, fluent lures in the victim’s own language and at scale. Microsoft’s Digital Defense Report 2025 found AI-automated phishing emails got a 54% click-through rate, versus 12% for standard ones. That is 4.5 times more effective, and Microsoft estimates AI can make phishing up to 50 times more profitable. Shadow AI is employees using AI tools the organization has not approved or cannot see. Pasting customer data into a public chatbot is the classic case. IBM’s 2025 report found high shadow AI use added $670,000 to the average breach cost. By the 2026 report , shadow AI was involved in 43% of the incidents IBM studied. An AI-orchestrated attack is one where an AI agent runs much of the intrusion itself, not just advises a human.

title: Architect Labs Unveils Frostbite, an Interaction Net CPU Designed by AI
abstract: Architect Labs has introduced Frostbite , an AI-designed CPU with a new instruction set built around interaction nets. The company states that its AI agents designed Frostbite from interaction net theory down to final GDS. In pre-silicon tests, it reports 4.59x the performance per watt of a modern in-order CPU core. Frostbite is a CPU from Architect Labs that executes programs as interaction nets in hardware. Programs are written in Vine , a Rust-like language, and compiled to an IR called Ivy. The chip is a mesh of tiles, each with its own small local memory. The launch post on X states that the AI agents co-designed the ISA and chip architecture given only interaction net theory. Interaction nets were introduced by Yves Lafont at POPL 1990 . A program is a graph of nodes. Computation rewrites pairs of nodes connected through their ports. Each node has 1 principal port, so active pairs never overlap and can fire in any order. Every value is used exactly once, so there is no shared mutable state to guard. A 5-queens net has 3,183 interactions and a 262-step critical path. About 12 interactions are ready per step. Software runtimes such as HVM2 already run interaction nets on GPUs. Frostbite moves the model into the ISA itself. The chip is built from tiles grouped into 2×2 quads. Each tile has front end, engine, memory and system blocks. A runtime domain adds a frame manager, scheduler, work queue and outlet. Its ISA adds wide bundles, hardware loop counters, streams, and ops that take, peek or copy values. Each tile runs its own queued work first. If idle, it takes work from a neighbor. If none is found, it goes inactive to save power. The company says this work stealing emerged during design and was not hand-specified. Agents first synthesized papers and built Python models. Their output was a 141-page PDF. It was deleted after the first RTL pass because its estimates were physically unrealistic. The research team then used ASL, an in-house, machine-checkable specification language. ASL is the single source of truth for the ISA, the Arcmodel system model, RTL and verification. The spec translates to Lean , and the project passed 800k lines of Lean. Arcmodel first diverged from RTL by almost 250% in the worst case. An automated fitting pipeline cut that to under 6% worst case and about 1.5% median. Arcmodel simulates the full chip 660x faster than RTL. Across 4 searches and an ablation round, agents tried 58 ideas and kept 37. The design targets 7 nm, timing at 800 MHz in synthesis and 500 MHz in final GDS. It follows Redwood , an edge AI accelerator the company announced in August 2026. The baseline is ‘TCPU,’ 1 core of a modern dual-issue, in-order superscalar CPU. Architect Labs does not name it, citing legal reasons. 1 Frostbite quad plus 4 L3 nodes occupies 0.792 mm². TCPU occupies 0.895 mm² on the same process. Across 25 workloads, geomean performance per watt is 4.59x. The 10-workload search set scores 6.02x, and the 15-workload held-out set 3.83x. Results range from 23.12x on conv2d to 1.15x on fib. Performance per area averages 8.77x. Fetch, decode and issue fall from 27% of TCPU energy to 6% in a quad. The on-chip network and scheduler take 26% instead. The fft, radixsort and LU kernels follow SPLASH-2 , scaled down 64x. Check out the full Frostbite technical post , the Vine language docs and Lafont’s original paper . You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . title: Meta TLX Brings Warp-Group GPU Control to Triton on Hopper, Blackwell, AMD
abstract: Meta has published a detailed report on TLX (Triton Low-Level Extensions) . It is the GPU compiler extension behind Meta’s production ML kernels. Meta TLX is a Triton extension that exposes warp groups, barriers, TMA and clusters to Python kernels. It targets NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell plus AMD MI300 and MI350-series GPUs. For kernel engineers, the message is CUDA-level control without leaving Triton. Triton programs GPUs at the block level. CUDA programs them at the thread level. Modern GPUs need something in between. Hopper introduced warp specialization and the Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA). Blackwell added tensor memory (TMEM), cluster execution and paired-CTA execution. Meta says CUDA could express these patterns, but only with large amounts of architecture-specific code. TLX fills that gap with a model the research team calls MIMW (Multi-Instruction, Multi-Warp) . The warp group becomes the basic unit of orchestration. Triton still defines what runs. TLX defines how it is orchestrated. Engineers write ordinary Triton and add TLX calls only where control matters. TLX adds 5 extension areas on top of Triton: The API reads like Triton. Meta’s Blackwell matmul example uses tlx.local_alloc , tlx.alloc_barriers , tlx.async_task , tlx.async_dot and tlx.barrier_wait . All figures below are self-reported by Meta: The research team adds that TLX trails state-of-the-art attention most on the smallest causal-forward cases. The gap narrows as sequence length grows. Meta’s engineering post lists 3 case studies: Meta also compared CUTLASS, CuTe DSL and TLX on Blackwell for GEM. It says TLX gave the best productivity-performance balance for most kernels, but shares no numbers. TLX lives in Meta’s MIT-licensed Triton fork, facebookexperimental/triton , under third_party/tlx/ . It also ships as triton-utlx on PyPI, a plugin for upstream Triton. The PyTorch-Triton 3.7 plugin system loads TLX without forking Triton. AMD has also published a GEMM plus activation guide for CDNA4 with TLX . Check out the paper on arXiv , the Meta engineering post and the GitHub repo . You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension .
